analysis.note: The supplied bhāṣya verse prints adyāḥ, but Sthiramati glosses ādyāḥ from ādau nirdiṣṭatvāt; this apparatus reads ādyāḥ, ‘first-mentioned’.
Sthiramati explicitly unpacks the compound as ‘those whose first is sparśa’; it denotes the five sarvatraga dharmas.

verification.detail: compound stem sparśādi as Pum/Prathama/Bahu: pass; relation bahuvrihi: unsupported (logged)

samasa.vigraha: chandaḥ ca adhimokṣaḥ ca smṛtiḥ ca

analysis.note: Final-member feminine morphology; semantically these three are counted with samādhi and dhī as five dharmas.

verification.detail: compound stem chandādhimokṣasmṛti as Stri/Prathama/Bahu: pass; relation dvandva: unsupported (logged)

analysis.note: Construes with the instrumental dual samādhidhībhyām.
Instrumental dual governed by saha; the compound uses final-member dhī morphology.

verification.detail: compound stem samādhidhī as Stri/Trtiya/Dvi: pass; relation dvandva: unsupported (logged)

analysis.note: Masculine plural understood with dharmāḥ; the commentary treats the class as viniyatāḥ, restricted to specific objects.
Printed together with atha as śraddhātha by vowel sandhi.
Marks the transition to the next, kuśala, set; in śraddhātha the initial a coalesces with the preceding ā.

justifications.decision: Read and translate the opening as ādyāḥ, ‘the first-mentioned ones,’ not as adyāḥ in any ordinary lexical sense; Sthiramati equates these first-mentioned factors with the sarvatraga class.
options_considered: adyāḥ as printed, from adya/ad
ādyāḥ merely as an ordinal ‘first’ with no technical force
ādyāḥ as ‘first-mentioned,’ meaning the universal/all-pervading factors

evidence.quote: ādau nirdiṣṭatvād ādyāḥ sarvatragā ity arthaḥ
evidence.translation: Because they were specified at the beginning, they are ‘the first’; the meaning is ‘the universal factors’.
The earlier verse passage listed contact, attention, etc.; thus they were specified first.

justifications.decision: Analyze sparśādayaḥ as a bahuvrīhi: ‘those whose first is contact,’ referring to the five universal mental factors, not to an indefinite open-ended ‘contact and so on’ without scope.
options_considered: simple loose ‘contact etc.’
tatpuruṣa with ādi as internal head only
bahuvrīhi ‘those whose beginning is contact,’ scoped to five sarvatraga dharmas
justifications.chosen: bahuvrīhi sparśaḥ ādiḥ eṣām; the five dharmas beginning with sparśa

evidence.quote: sparśamanaskārādayaḥ pañca dharmāḥ sarvacittam anugacchantīti sarvatragāḥ
evidence.translation: The five dharmas beginning with contact and attention accompany every mind; therefore they are universal.

evidence.quote:
tathā hy eta ālayavijñāne kliṣṭe manasi pravṛttivijñāneṣu cāviśeṣeṇa
pravartante
evidence.translation: For they occur without distinction in ālayavijñāna, afflicted manas, and the active consciousnesses.

justifications.decision: Construe chandādhimokṣasmṛtayaḥ with saha samādhidhībhyām as a set of five niyata/viniyata dharmas; samādhi and dhī are included by saha with the preceding triple.
options_considered: only the three in chandādhimokṣasmṛtayaḥ are niyatāḥ
samādhidhībhyām is an incidental instrumental not counted in the set
three plus samādhi and dhī form five determinate dharmas
justifications.chosen: chanda, adhimokṣa, smṛti, together with samādhi and dhī, are the five viniyata dharmas

evidence.quote:
viniyatān adhikṛtyāha
chandādhimokṣasmṛtayaḥ saha
samādhidhībhyāṃ niyatāḥ
evidence.translation: With reference to the determinate/restricted ones he says: desire, ascertainment, and mindfulness, together with concentration and discernment, are niyata.

evidence.quote:
ete hi pañca dharmāḥ parasparaṃ vyatiricyāpi pravartante
evañ ca
yatrādhimokṣas tatra nāvaśyam itarair api bhavitavyam
evaṃ sarvatra vācyam
evidence.translation: These are five dharmas, and they occur even separately from one another; where adhimokṣa is present, the others need not necessarily be present. This should be said throughout.

justifications.decision: Translate niyatāḥ in this context as ‘determinate/restricted,’ i.e. having specific objects, not as ‘permanent,’ ‘necessary,’ or ‘always present.’
options_considered: fixed in the sense of permanent
necessary/inevitable
restricted to a particular object-domain
justifications.chosen: restricted/determinate: viśeṣe niyata, with a specific object rather than every object

evidence.quote:
viśeṣe niyatatvād viniyatāḥ
eṣāṃ hi viśeṣa eva viṣayo na sarvaḥ
evidence.translation: They are ‘restricted’ because they are fixed on a specific case; for their object is only something specific, not everything.

justifications.decision: Translate chanda as aspiration/desire toward an intended object, not as ‘metre’ or a general preference without object-restriction.
options_considered: metre
desire in general
aspiration/desire for an intended object

evidence.quote:
tatra chando 'bhiprete vastuny abhilāṣaḥ
abhiprete vastuny abhilāṣa iti
pratiniyataviṣayatvaṃ jñāpitaṃ bhavaty anabhiprete chandābhāvāt
darśanaśravaṇādikriyāviṣayatvena yad abhimataṃ vastu tad abhipretam
tatra
darśanaśravaṇādiprārthanā chandaḥ
sa ca vīryārambhasaṃniśrayadānakarmakaḥ
evidence.translation: Chanda is desire for an intended object; saying ‘for an intended object’ shows its specifically determined object, since chanda is absent toward what is not intended. It is the wishing for seeing, hearing, and the like, and it has the function of giving support for the undertaking of vigor.

justifications.decision: Translate adhimokṣa as ascertainment/resolve toward a decided object, not as liberation or release.
options_considered: release/liberation
belief without certainty
ascertainment or firm resolve toward what is decided
justifications.chosen: ascertainment/resolve (adhimokṣa) with respect to a niścita vastu

evidence.quote:
adhimokṣo niścite vastuni tathaivāvadhāraṇam
niścitagrahaṇam
aniścitapratiṣedhārtham
yuktita āptopadeśato vā yad vastu asaṃdigdhaṃ tan
niścitam
yenaivākāreṇa tan niścitam anityaduḥkhādyākāreṇa tenaivākāreṇa
tasya vastunaś cetasy abhiniveśanam
evam etan nānyathety avadhāraṇam
adhimokṣaḥ
sa cāsaṃhāryatākarmakaḥ
evidence.translation: Adhimokṣa is determination just so with respect to a decided object; ‘decided’ excludes the undecided. What is free from doubt through reasoning or authoritative instruction is decided. Fixing that object in mind in just the way it is decided—‘it is thus, not otherwise’—is adhimokṣa; its function is non-removability.

justifications.decision: Translate smṛti as mindfulness/recollection, specifically the non-loss and mental re-expression of a familiar or previously experienced object, not as a text or sacred tradition.
options_considered: scriptural tradition
mere memory in an unspecified sense
mindfulness/recollection as non-loss of a previously experienced object

evidence.quote:
smṛtiḥ saṃstute vastuny asaṃpramoṣaś cetaso 'bhilapanatā
saṃstutaṃ vastu
pūrvānubhūtam
ālambanagrahaṇāvipraṇāśakāraṇatvād asaṃpramoṣaḥ
pūrvagṛhītasya vastunaḥ punaḥ punar ālambanākārasmaraṇam abhilapanatā
abhilapanam evābhilapanatā
sā punar avikṣepakarmikā
evidence.translation: Smṛti is non-loss with respect to a familiar object and the mind’s abhilapanatā; the familiar object is one previously experienced. It is non-loss because it causes the grasping of the object not to perish; abhilapanatā is repeatedly remembering the object-aspect of what was previously grasped. Its function is non-distraction.

justifications.decision: Translate samādhi as concentration/single-pointedness and dhī as discernment/prajñā, not as generic ‘putting together’ and ‘thought.’
options_considered: samādhi as mere joining; dhī as thought in general
samādhi as meditative concentration; dhī as discernment/prajñā that investigates dharmas

evidence.quote:
samādhir upaparīkṣye vastuni cittasyaikāgratā
upaparīkṣyaṃ vastu guṇato
doṣato vā
ekāgratā ekālambanatā
jñānasaṃniśrayadānakarmakaḥ
samāhite
citte yathābhūtaparijñānāt
evidence.translation: Samādhi is the mind’s single-pointedness with respect to an object to be examined, whether in terms of qualities or faults; single-pointedness is having one object, and it supports knowledge, since true comprehension occurs in a concentrated mind.

evidence.quote:
dhīḥ prajñā
sāpy upaparīkṣya eva vastuni pravicayo yogāyogavihito 'nyathā
veti
pravicinotīti pravicayaḥ
yaḥ samyaṅ mithyā vā
saṃkīrṇasvasāmānyalakṣaṇeṣv iva dharmeṣu vivekāvabodhaḥ
evidence.translation: Dhī is prajñā. It is investigation of an examinable object, produced by proper means, improper means, or otherwise. Pravicaya is what investigates; whether correct or mistaken, it is discriminating understanding among dharmas with mixed own- and common-characteristics.

evidence.quote:
eṣā ca saṃśayavyāvartanakarmikā
saṃśayavyāvartanaṃ prajñayā dharmān pravicinvato niścayalābhād iti
evidence.translation: Its function is the removal of doubt, since one gains certainty when investigating dharmas by prajñā.

justifications.decision: Take śraddhā atha hrīḥ apatrapā as the beginning of the next kuśala list, not as further items governed by niyatāḥ.
options_considered: faith, shame, and apatrapā are also niyatāḥ
atha is merely ornamental
atha marks the next set, the wholesome factors
justifications.chosen: atha introduces the immediately following kuśala dharmas, beginning with śraddhā, hrī, and apatrapā

evidence.quote:
uktā viniyatāḥ
tadanantaroddiṣṭās tv idānīṃ kuśalā vaktavyā ity ata āha
śraddhātha hrīr apatrapā
evidence.translation: The restricted ones have been stated. Now the wholesome factors specified immediately after them are to be stated; therefore he says: faith, then shame, apatrapā.

translation:
The first-mentioned—contact (sparśa) and the rest—are the universal factors (sarvatraga);
aspiration (chanda), ascertainment (adhimokṣa), and mindfulness (smṛti),
together with concentration (samādhi) and discernment (dhī), are the determinate/restricted ones (niyata/viniyata).
Then: faith (śraddhā), shame (hrī), and compunction (apatrapā).
one_shot_delta: A commentary-blind translation might take the supplied adyāḥ at face value; Sthiramati’s gloss requires ādyāḥ, ‘first-mentioned,’ and equates it with sarvatraga.
It might leave sparśādayaḥ as a vague ‘contact etc.’; the commentary fixes it as the five all-pervading factors beginning with contact.
It might read niyatāḥ as ‘necessary’ or ‘always present’; Sthiramati defines the class by restriction to specific objects, not by constant occurrence.
It might fail to count samādhi and dhī with the preceding triple; saha plus the commentary yields five viniyata dharmas.
It might make śraddhā, hrī, and apatrapā part of the niyata predicate; Sthiramati marks a new kuśala list at atha.
analyzer_disagreements: ByT5 analyzes the opening as adyāḥ with lemma adya/ad; Sthiramati’s ādau nirdiṣṭatvād ādyāḥ requires ādyāḥ from ādya ‘first-mentioned.’ I therefore override the analyzer and record the printed form separately as surface_in_sandhi.
open_questions: Within the permitted verse-10 commentary span, śraddhā, hrī, and apatrapā are identified only as the start of the kuśala list; their detailed definitions belong to the following verse’s commentary, so the English glosses for hrī and apatrapā are conventional rather than line-glossed here.
